report:
**Conclusion:** Your view is not supported by the strongest direct evidence. Chlorhexidine–alcohol *does* appear to reduce cesarean surgical-site infection (SSI) versus iodine–alcohol, although the evidence base is not uniformly positive and the absolute benefit is modest.

The pivotal multicenter randomized trial found SSI in 23/572 (4.0%) with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus 42/575 (7.3%) with iodine–alcohol—an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points (roughly 1 fewer infection per 30 preparations), statistically significant. This is the most relevant comparison to the claim because both preparations contained alcohol.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

A cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded that chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced SSI compared with povidone–iodine preparations.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/

**Evidence supporting skepticism:** A randomized CAPICA trial found no SSI advantage for chlorhexidine–alcohol over *aqueous* povidone–iodine scrub-and-paint. But that is not the claimed iodine–alcohol comparison: alcohol itself is an important antiseptic component, so this result does not directly contradict the pivotal trial.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/

A smaller 311-person pilot trial also favored chlorhexidine–alcohol numerically but did not reach statistical significance, consistent with insufficient power rather than proof of no effect.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/

Thus, it would be fair to say certainty is limited by relatively few direct trials and varying formulations/protocols. But “chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI compared with iodine–alcohol” is a well-supported claim, not a false one.
